nodes.title: ROS 2 计算图
nodes.summary: Nodes expose typed interfaces; processes and nodes are different organizational units.
nodes.definition: A ROS 2 computation graph describes participating nodes and their communication interfaces. A node is a named unit of computation, such as a camera driver, estimator, or controller; several nodes may share a process, and one process may contain several execution threads. Publishers, subscriptions, service endpoints, and action endpoints belong to nodes. Discovery finds compatible participants, while an executor schedules callbacks in a client-library application. This graph organizes software communication. It is distinct from a neural-network computation graph, a physical robot kinematic tree, and a SLAM factor graph.
nodes.example: A camera node publishes images, a detector subscribes to them, and a tracker consumes detections. Moving the detector into another process changes deployment and failure isolation, but need not change its topic interface. Record node names, message types, callback execution, and process placement separately when debugging missed updates.
nodes.role_en: Provides the software structure connecting sensors, estimation, learned models, planners, and robot interfaces.

notation.meaning: Set of participating ROS nodes.
Communication relationships; this notation summarizes architecture rather than a ROS API.

nodes.title: 话题与消息
nodes.summary: Typed publish/subscribe streams carry observations, states, and commands.
nodes.definition: A topic provides asynchronous, typed publish/subscribe communication. Publishers send messages under a topic name; subscriptions receive compatible messages without requiring direct knowledge of the publishing node. A message definition specifies fields and their types. Sensor streams commonly include a measurement timestamp and frame identifier, whose meanings must be preserved through processing. A topic can have multiple publishers and subscribers. Reception still depends on middleware discovery, compatible QoS, scheduling, and network behavior; publishing a message does not establish that a controller received or acted on it.
nodes.example: An image topic carries an image together with its acquisition time and camera frame. A detector publishes bounding boxes with that same measurement time rather than replacing it with inference completion time. A recorder and tracker can subscribe independently, allowing replay without modifying the camera driver.
nodes.role_en: Supplies the transport interface for sensor pipelines, state estimates, and command streams.

notation.meaning: Conceptual message at index k.
Measurement timestamp; its semantics depend on the message and driver.

nodes.title: 服务与动作
nodes.summary: Services return short request results; actions track long-running goals.
nodes.definition: A service is a request/response interface intended for operations that complete promptly. An action represents a longer-running goal with feedback, a terminal result, and cancellation support. Their interface definitions specify different message sections: request and response for services; goal, result, and feedback for actions. Cancellation is a protocol request whose handling depends on the server; it is not proof of an immediate physical stop. These communication patterns should be selected according to task semantics, with the actuator-level stop behavior implemented and checked independently.
nodes.example: Querying a calibration parameter can use a service. Navigating to a field position can use an action that reports remaining progress and accepts cancellation. If the player cancels navigation, the server transitions its goal state and separately commands a valid stopping behavior through the controller interface.
nodes.role_en: Connects task-level commands and progress monitoring to the continuous sensor and control streams.

notation.meaning: Request and response/result.
Action goal and successive feedback messages; notation is conceptual.

nodes.en: DDS and ROS 2 Quality of Service
nodes.title: DDS 与通信质量
nodes.summary: Reliability, history, durability, and timing policies affect whether data arrives usefully.
nodes.definition: ROS 2 exposes middleware Quality of Service policies that configure communication behavior. Common DDS-backed deployments support reliability, history/depth, durability, deadline, lifespan, and liveliness policies. Publishers offer policies and subscribers request policies; incompatible combinations may prevent communication. Reliable transport can retransmit data, while best-effort delivery can discard losses; neither choice guarantees a timely control update. Queue depth and stale-message handling must match whether the application needs the newest observation or every sample. Middleware selection and supported policies should be checked for the actual ROS distribution.
nodes.example: A live camera consumer may prefer recent frames over a growing backlog. A map subscriber may need the most recently published map immediately after joining, motivating suitable durability. Inspect compatibility and message age before blaming an estimator when a topic is visible but delivers no usable measurements.
nodes.role_en: Explains communication failures, stale observations, and queue behavior in deployed perception and control systems.

notation.meaning: Age of an observation when used; clocks must be comparable.
Time at which a consumer uses the sample.

nodes.title: 坐标变换树
nodes.summary: Transforms must match both the coordinate frame and measurement time.
nodes.definition: tf2 maintains time-buffered transforms between named coordinate frames organized as a tree. A rigid transform converts coordinates of the same physical point between frames. Static sensor mounts use fixed transforms; moving joints or robot poses require time-dependent transforms. A lookup must request a time for which the required transform chain is available. Frame conventions distinguish a locally continuous but drifting odom frame from a globally corrected map frame. An available transform does not establish that its calibration or localization estimate is accurate.
nodes.example: A ball position measured in camera coordinates at exposure time is transformed into base coordinates using the camera-to-base transform at that exposure time. If the head turned during inference, using the latest transform instead can place the ball incorrectly even when its image detection is correct.
nodes.role_en: Connects camera/LiDAR observations, robot kinematics, odometry, maps, and controller targets.

notation.meaning: Rigid transform mapping B-frame homogeneous coordinates into frame A.
Homogeneous point coordinates; all transforms must refer to compatible times.

sources.title: REP-105: Coordinate Frames for Mobile Platforms

nodes.title: 时钟与同步
nodes.summary: Acquisition time, arrival time, and computation completion are different events.
nodes.definition: A measurement timestamp should identify the physical acquisition event in a defined clock domain. Arrival and processing completion occur later and can vary with transport and computation. Multiple sensors may have clock offsets, drift, exposure intervals, and device-specific stamping rules. ROS time can follow a simulation or replay clock and may pause or jump; a steady clock supports measuring elapsed durations without wall-clock adjustments. Synchronization pairs observations in time but does not remove unknown acquisition delay. Calibration and interpolation must respect these distinctions.
nodes.example: An image arrives after its exposure, while several IMU samples have already arrived. The estimator uses acquisition timestamps to integrate IMU measurements over the image interval. Replaying the same bag with simulated ROS time requires consistent use of that clock, rather than comparing its stamps with the computer wall clock.
nodes.role_en: Prevents incorrect fusion, transforms, latency measurements, and reproducibility during bag replay and simulation.

notation.meaning: Clock scale/drift and offset in an affine clock model.
Transport and buffering delay, potentially time varying.

nodes.title: 控制器与硬件接口
nodes.summary: A read–update–write cycle connects controllers to measured states and command interfaces.
nodes.definition: ros2_control is a ROS 2 framework separating hardware access from controller implementations. Hardware components export state and command interfaces, such as measured joint position and commanded effort. A controller manager coordinates controller lifecycle and interface ownership, while its update loop reads hardware, updates controllers, and writes commands. Supported interfaces, timing, limits, and failure handling depend on the robot plugin and configuration. This framework does not provide a universal stabilizing policy: a humanoid still requires a suitable whole-body controller or learned locomotion policy and a validated hardware integration.
nodes.example: A joint controller reads encoder position and velocity and writes an effort command through a hardware plugin. An upper-level policy may supply position targets instead. The configuration must identify which controller owns each interface, avoid conflicting writers, and verify units and timing before any physical experiment.
nodes.role_en: Bridges software algorithms and robot actuators without conflating a ROS command with realized physical motion.

notation.meaning: Read hardware state.
Command written through the selected command interface.

nodes.title: 相机内参与投影
nodes.summary: Image pixels are rays; metric depth requires additional information.
nodes.definition: A pinhole camera maps a three-dimensional point in its camera frame to image coordinates by dividing its horizontal and vertical coordinates by depth. Intrinsics encode focal lengths and principal point in pixel units. Real cameras require a distortion model, and fisheye lenses may use a different projection family. Calibration estimates model parameters from known geometry and observations. A single pixel generally determines a viewing ray rather than a unique metric point. Depth, stereo, known object geometry, or other constraints are required to recover distance.
nodes.example: A ball center at pixel coordinates is converted into a camera-frame ray after distortion correction. To estimate a ground intersection, the system additionally needs camera pose and a ground-plane assumption. An airborne ball violates that assumption, so image detection accuracy alone cannot establish accurate three-dimensional ball position.
nodes.role_en: Provides the observation geometry used by visual odometry, visual-inertial estimation, reconstruction, and ball localization.

notation.meaning: Point coordinates in the camera frame, with positive visible depth.
Focal lengths and principal point; formula omits distortion.

sources.title: OpenCV: Camera calibration and 3D reconstruction API source

nodes.title: 传感器外参标定
nodes.summary: Sensor measurements need measured transforms into the robot frame.
nodes.definition: Extrinsic calibration estimates the rigid transformation between sensor coordinate frames or between a sensor and the robot body. Rotation and translation must be interpreted with an explicit mapping direction and consistent units. A CAD or URDF mount transform is a geometric specification; calibration tests the actual installation, including mounting errors. Multi-sensor calibration can estimate parameters by minimizing disagreement between observations of common structure. Transform uncertainty propagates into reconstructed positions. Flexing mounts, moving joints, and sensor relocation can invalidate a previously calibrated fixed transform.
nodes.example: Estimate the camera-to-base transform from calibration observations and check it against independent target positions. A small angular error can create a substantial position error at long range. If the camera sits on a moving head, combine its fixed mount calibration with the head joint kinematics at the measurement time.
nodes.role_en: Makes different sensor outputs physically comparable and links perception to robot control coordinates.

notation.meaning: Rotation and translation mapping camera coordinates into base coordinates.
Coordinates of the same point in camera and base frames.

sources.title: REP-103: Standard Units and Coordinate Conventions

nodes.en: IMU Specific Force, Bias, and Integration
nodes.title: 惯性测量与偏置
nodes.summary: Accelerometers measure specific force; bias causes integration drift.
nodes.definition: An IMU combines gyroscope angular-rate measurements with accelerometer specific-force measurements. Specific force is not directly world-frame linear acceleration: gravity and orientation must be handled using the chosen convention. Measurements also contain bias and noise, and biases can vary over time. Integration propagates orientation, velocity, and position between other observations, but its errors accumulate. An IMU alone generally cannot maintain drift-free global position. Noise density, sample rate, saturation, mounting orientation, and acquisition timestamps must be obtained from the actual sensor configuration.
nodes.example: A stationary level IMU typically reports a nonzero accelerometer vector because its support force balances gravity. The estimator rotates the measured specific force into the world frame and adds the world gravity vector to obtain linear acceleration. A small uncorrected accelerometer bias then accumulates into velocity and position error.
nodes.role_en: Supplies short-term motion propagation for VIO, LiDAR-inertial odometry, and robot state estimation.

notation.meaning: Rotation from IMU frame to world frame.
Gyroscope and accelerometer biases.
Measured specific force; g_W is world-frame gravity.

sources.title: VINS-Mono: A Robust and Versatile Monocular Visual-Inertial State Estimator

nodes.en: LiDAR Point Clouds and Motion De-skewing
nodes.title: 激光点云与运动补偿
nodes.summary: A scan contains points acquired at different times, not necessarily one rigid instant.
nodes.definition: A LiDAR measures ranges along emitted directions and produces points in a sensor coordinate frame. Spinning and solid-state sensors have different scan patterns, fields of view, and acquisition timing. A scan assembled while the robot moves contains points measured from different sensor poses. De-skewing uses estimated motion and point timestamps to express those observations at a common reference time. Accuracy depends on timing, extrinsic calibration, scene geometry, and the motion estimate. Reflectivity, occlusion, range limits, and moving objects also affect which returns can constrain robot pose.
nodes.example: A humanoid turns while scanning a wall. Without compensation, the assembled wall can appear bent. Use each point time and interpolated body motion to express points in the scan-start frame. This requires the driver point-time convention and does not remove errors caused by incorrect motion estimates or moving people.
nodes.role_en: Prepares geometrically consistent measurements for scan registration and LiDAR-inertial odometry.

notation.meaning: Point acquisition time and selected scan reference time.
LiDAR pose in world coordinates at time t.

nodes.title: 标定可观测性
nodes.summary: A low residual cannot identify parameters that the recorded motion does not constrain.
nodes.definition: Observability asks whether different hidden states or parameters can be distinguished from the available measurements and motion. Calibration may optimize camera-IMU rotation, translation, time offset, and biases, but some motions leave certain parameters weakly constrained. Linearization exposes this through the rank or singular values of a sensitivity matrix after appropriate gauge freedoms are accounted for. A small fitting residual can coexist with inaccurate parameters. Independent validation, sufficient motion variation, realistic noise assumptions, and parameter uncertainty are therefore necessary when judging calibration quality.
nodes.example: Collecting only nearly static camera-IMU data provides little evidence about time offset because shifting timestamps hardly changes predicted observations. Include controlled rotational and translational variation suitable for the calibration method, then evaluate held-out data. Do not interpret successful optimizer termination as proof that every extrinsic parameter was identified.
nodes.role_en: Explains why calibration and state estimation require informative motion and why some errors persist despite optimization.

notation.meaning: Measurement sensitivity to calibration parameters.
Local information approximation; rank deficiency indicates locally unconstrained directions.
Measurement weighting matrix.

sources.title: VINS-Mono: A Robust and Versatile Monocular Visual-Inertial State Estimator

nodes.title: 里程计与局部运动
nodes.summary: Incremental motion estimates can be continuous while drifting globally.
nodes.definition: Odometry estimates a robot trajectory from successive local motion observations, such as wheel encoders, image correspondences, LiDAR scans, or inertial measurements. Relative transforms are composed to obtain pose over time. Small systematic and random errors accumulate, creating drift. In ROS conventions, an odom frame is locally continuous but may drift without bound; a map frame may receive global corrections and therefore change discontinuously. Odometry, localization against a known map, and SLAM solve related but different estimation problems, and should not be treated as interchangeable outputs.
nodes.example: A robot walks around a closed corridor and local odometry returns near, but not exactly to, its starting pose. The controller can still use the smooth local estimate for short motions. A verified loop closure or external localization measurement can correct global position without making the original incremental estimates error-free.
nodes.role_en: Connects sensor motion measurements to local feedback and provides trajectory constraints for SLAM.

notation.meaning: Estimated incremental pose mapping coordinates at step k+1 into frame k.
Accumulated pose relative to a chosen world origin.

sources.title: REP-105: Coordinate Frames for Mobile Platforms

nodes.title: 视觉惯性里程计
nodes.summary: Jointly estimate motion, gravity-related quantities, and IMU biases from images and inertial data.
nodes.definition: Visual-inertial odometry combines camera observations with IMU measurements to estimate a local trajectory. Images constrain relative geometric motion through feature observations or photometric alignment, while the IMU supplies motion propagation between exposures. Tightly coupled methods optimize or filter these measurements within a joint state containing pose, velocity, and biases. Metric scale can become observable under suitable motion and assumptions, unlike unconstrained monocular visual geometry. Initialization, synchronization, extrinsics, texture, lighting, rolling shutter, and motion excitation strongly affect performance. VIO without global corrections remains an odometry system and can drift.
nodes.example: As a robot turns its head, IMU angular motion helps predict feature movement between images. Reprojection residuals correct the propagated pose and biases. A plain wall or severe blur weakens visual constraints; the IMU can bridge short intervals but cannot supply indefinitely accurate position during visual failure.
nodes.role_en: Introduces the sensor combination underlying ORB-SLAM3 inertial modes and many mobile-robot localization pipelines.

notation.meaning: States and, depending on method, landmarks or calibration parameters.
Mahalanobis squared residual r transpose Sigma inverse r; schematic objective, not a unique VIO implementation.

sources.title: VINS-Mono: A Robust and Versatile Monocular Visual-Inertial State Estimator

nodes.title: 激光惯性里程计
nodes.summary: IMU propagation and geometric scan constraints jointly estimate body motion.
nodes.definition: LiDAR-inertial odometry combines inertial propagation with geometric constraints from LiDAR returns. IMU measurements help predict motion and compensate acquisition distortion; point-to-map or feature-based registration corrects that prediction. Tightly coupled approaches estimate pose, velocity, biases, and sometimes extrinsics within a shared estimator. Filter-based and smoothing-based implementations organize computation differently. Performance depends on scene geometry: a long featureless corridor or a sparse distant scene can leave motion directions weakly constrained. A local LIO map does not by itself imply loop closure or globally drift-free SLAM.
nodes.example: A robot moves through a room containing walls at several orientations. LiDAR point-to-plane residuals constrain pose while the IMU predicts movement between scans. In a geometrically repetitive corridor, inspect directional uncertainty and registration failures rather than assuming that a visually dense point cloud determines all six motion dimensions.
nodes.role_en: Connects LiDAR geometry and IMU models to FAST-LIO2 and LIO-SAM without conflating odometry with complete navigation.

notation.meaning: LiDAR point after appropriate timing compensation.
Matched map-plane point and unit normal.
Candidate point-to-map transform; residual is point-to-plane distance.

nodes.title: 因子图与稀疏平滑
nodes.summary: A factor connects the unknown variables involved in one measurement or prior.
nodes.definition: A factor graph is a bipartite graph with variable nodes and factor nodes. Variables can represent robot poses, velocities, sensor biases, or landmarks. Each factor expresses a measurement likelihood or prior involving a subset of variables. Maximum a posteriori estimation combines these terms; Gaussian error models lead to a weighted nonlinear least-squares objective. Smoothing estimates multiple historical states together, allowing later observations to revise earlier poses. Sparsity comes from local factor dependencies. Gauge freedom, initialization, robust losses, and incorrect associations must be handled; drawing a graph does not resolve them.
nodes.example: A trajectory graph contains one pose variable per selected keyframe. Adjacent keyframes receive odometry factors, and a known landmark adds a measurement factor. Optimizing all these constraints adjusts several poses together. A first-pose prior or another appropriate reference removes the arbitrary global coordinate choice for the selected formulation.
nodes.role_en: Expands the existing SLAM overview into the estimation structure used by smoothing, bundle adjustment, and LIO-SAM.

notation.meaning: Subset of variables participating in factor i.
Measurement or prior factor.
Residual and its covariance in the Gaussian least-squares case.

sources.title: Factor Graphs and GTSAM: A Hands-on Introduction

nodes.title: 地点识别与回环
nodes.summary: Recognizing a place proposes a constraint; geometric verification decides whether to use it.
nodes.definition: Loop closure adds a nonlocal relation between states recorded when a robot revisits a place. Place recognition proposes candidates from visual or geometric similarity; geometric verification checks that observations support a consistent relative pose. A pose-graph or other back-end then distributes the correction across its connected states. Repeated corridors, changing environments, dynamic objects, and perceptual aliasing can create false candidates. Robust estimation can reduce some bad-constraint effects but cannot guarantee correctness. Relocalization recovers pose against an existing map and is related to, but distinct from, closing a trajectory loop.
nodes.example: A robot observes a goal area that resembles the opposite end of a soccer field. Appearance retrieval alone can confuse them. Require geometric consistency and appropriate contextual checks before adding a loop constraint; otherwise the map may be corrected toward the wrong end even though the optimizer converges.
nodes.role_en: Explains how global SLAM corrections extend drifting local odometry and why false loop closures are consequential.

notation.meaning: Verified relative-pose measurement between keyframes i and j.
Estimated poses in a shared map frame.
Local Lie-group logarithm converting pose error to a tangent vector.

sources.title: Factor Graphs and GTSAM: A Hands-on Introduction

nodes.title: 占据栅格与八叉树
nodes.summary: Free, occupied, and unobserved space have different meanings.
nodes.definition: An occupancy map divides space into cells and estimates whether each cell contains an obstacle. Range observations support occupied endpoints and free space along traversed rays, while unobserved regions remain unknown. Log-odds updates conveniently combine evidence under the chosen inverse sensor and independence approximations. A two-dimensional grid suits some planar navigation tasks; an octree represents three-dimensional occupancy at multiple spatial scales. Resolution, sensor error, moving obstacles, and map aging affect usefulness. Absence of a return is not universally equivalent to free space, especially with range limits or sensor failure.
nodes.example: A LiDAR ray crosses several cells before returning from a wall. The map marks traversed visible cells as free evidence and the endpoint as occupied evidence. Space behind the wall remains unknown. A planner must explicitly choose how to treat unknown space rather than interpreting every unfilled cell as traversable.
nodes.role_en: Connects range measurements and probabilistic updates to collision checking and map-based navigation.

notation.meaning: Occupancy log odds of cell c after update t.
Prior log odds; update assumes a compatible inverse sensor model.

nodes.en: TSDF and Euclidean Signed Distance Fields
nodes.title: 截断与欧氏符号距离场
nodes.summary: Surface reconstruction and nearest-obstacle distance serve different downstream uses.
nodes.definition: A signed distance field assigns distance values relative to a surface under a stated sign convention. A TSDF fuses truncated distance observations near surfaces and supports reconstruction; its stored values are not generally exact Euclidean nearest-obstacle distances. An ESDF approximates Euclidean distance to the nearest surface and can provide gradients for trajectory optimization. Construction must distinguish observed free space from unknown space, update changed geometry, and select resolution. Planning also needs robot geometry and margins; a positive distance at the robot center alone does not establish collision-free whole-body motion.
nodes.example: A reconstructed wall can be displayed as a mesh from a TSDF. A trajectory optimizer instead queries ESDF distance and gradient at sampled robot body points to penalize nearby obstacles. The body radius or shape, map uncertainty, and unobserved regions remain part of collision-checking assumptions.
nodes.role_en: Provides geometric costs for collision-aware trajectory optimization and local planning.

notation.meaning: Represented obstacle surface.
Sign convention, positive in modeled free space here.
Example clearance threshold; cost is illustrative, not the Voxblox algorithm.

sources.title: Voxblox: Incremental 3D Euclidean Signed Distance Fields for On-Board MAV Planning

nodes.title: 导航系统分工
nodes.summary: A navigation stack coordinates estimates, maps, routes, local commands, and recovery.
nodes.definition: A navigation stack combines localization, environmental representations, global planning, local control, and task execution. Localization estimates robot pose; a planner searches for a route; a local controller generates commands using nearby obstacles and motion constraints. Costmaps translate sensed geometry into planning costs, while behaviors or task logic manage failures and goal progression. Nav2 supplies these interfaces and implementations in ROS 2. A mobile-base navigation command does not automatically provide dynamically stable humanoid locomotion: the command must be realized by a suitable lower-level controller, with robot geometry and operating assumptions checked.
nodes.example: A high-level task requests a field waypoint. The global planner selects a route around an obstacle, the local controller issues velocity targets, and a locomotion controller realizes them. A falling risk or invalid localization estimate requires handling across these layers; a successful route search alone does not imply successful physical arrival.
nodes.role_en: Positions SLAM, mapping, classical planning, and learned locomotion within one robotics architecture.

notation.meaning: Route in a map or planning representation.
Interface-level command subject to downstream controller capability.

nodes.title: 目标检测与观测几何
nodes.summary: A class label and image box are measurements, not a full physical state.
nodes.definition: Object detection predicts object categories and image regions, often bounding boxes and confidence scores. Detection confidence is not automatically a calibrated probability of metric localization accuracy. A detector may miss occluded objects, confuse similar objects, or produce biased centers. Converting a box or mask into a three-dimensional position requires additional geometry, depth, calibration, or an explicit object model. Training distributions, annotation conventions, and camera conditions affect performance. Detection is a per-observation perception stage; temporal identity, velocity, and uncertainty require additional estimation machinery.
nodes.example: A soccer detector returns a ball box. Its pixel center defines a viewing direction after camera calibration. Estimate distance using validated depth or geometry, and propagate relevant uncertainty. Track errors separately for visible-ball detection, pixel localization, metric position, and downstream control so one success metric does not conceal another failure.
nodes.role_en: Supplies object observations for tracking and interaction while separating recognition from state estimation.

notation.meaning: Predicted image box, category, and confidence score.
Back-projection to a ray under the calibrated camera model, not a unique 3D point.

sources.title: Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks

nodes.title: 数据关联与门控
nodes.summary: Determine which observation belongs to which tracked object or landmark.
nodes.definition: Data association assigns incoming observations to existing tracks or landmarks, while permitting new objects, missed detections, and rejected measurements. Motion uncertainty defines a predicted measurement distribution; a Mahalanobis gate rejects observations inconsistent with that prediction. Assignment can also use appearance, class, geometry, and one-to-one constraints. A small residual is not definitive identity evidence when multiple objects are similar or nearby. Incorrect associations can corrupt a tracker or SLAM estimate. Gating thresholds and covariance calibration therefore affect both rejected correct measurements and accepted incorrect ones.
nodes.example: Two balls or ball-like highlights appear near a predicted ball location. Gate candidates using the tracker covariance, then evaluate additional appearance and geometric evidence. If ambiguity remains, retain uncertainty or mark the estimate unreliable instead of silently switching identity and reporting a highly confident velocity.
nodes.role_en: Links raw detections to temporal tracking and feature correspondences used in localization.

notation.meaning: Candidate measurement and predicted measurement in the same representation.
Innovation covariance.
Gate threshold selected for the model and desired rejection behavior.

sources.title: Deep SORT: Simple Online and Realtime Tracking with a Deep Association Metric

nodes.en: Object Tracking, Occlusion, and Ball State
nodes.title: 目标跟踪与遮挡
nodes.summary: Predict state between measurements while exposing uncertainty and model limits.
nodes.definition: Object tracking estimates a temporal state, such as position and velocity, from incomplete noisy observations. A motion model predicts forward; accepted measurements update that prediction. During occlusion or missed detections, uncertainty should grow according to the process model, and the output should identify its observation age. A constant-velocity model is useful over limited intervals but does not describe every bounce, kick, rolling-friction change, or collision. Robot motion must be removed or modeled when interpreting camera-relative measurements. Track persistence and confident physical state are different claims.
nodes.example: A ball disappears behind a leg. The tracker briefly predicts its field-frame position with growing covariance and labels the estimate as unobserved. A later detection is gated before updating. If a kick occurred during occlusion, the old constant-velocity prediction may be wrong and should not be trusted as an observed trajectory.
nodes.role_en: Connects perception to interception, passing, and closed-loop control with explicit visibility and uncertainty.

notation.meaning: Position and velocity in an explicitly selected common frame.
Process noise representing unmodeled acceleration; constant-velocity baseline only.

sources.title: Deep SORT: Simple Online and Realtime Tracking with a Deep Association Metric

nodes.title: 观测延迟与补偿
nodes.summary: Control uses a delayed estimate unless acquisition-to-action timing is accounted for.
nodes.definition: End-to-end latency spans acquisition, transfer, queuing, preprocessing, inference, estimation, planning, command transport, and actuator response. Throughput counts completed work per time; it is different from the age of a particular observation when its resulting command acts. Time-stamped state prediction can compensate some delay under a valid dynamics model, but cannot recover unseen events or eliminate prediction error. Tail latency, dropped frames, changing queues, and mismatched clocks matter alongside averages. A measured pipeline budget is needed before claiming that faster inference improves closed-loop behavior.
nodes.example: For an illustrative constant-speed ball moving at two meters per second, a 0.1-second old position differs by about 0.2 meters along its motion. Predicting forward can reduce this offset if velocity is accurate. A bounce during that interval invalidates the simple prediction even when the arithmetic is correct.
nodes.role_en: Links timestamping and tracking to real-time planning, asynchronous inference, and physical action timing.

notation.meaning: Measured observation-to-use delay with compatible clocks.
First-order displacement under a constant-velocity assumption, not a universal error bound.

nodes.title: 实时期限与指令约束
nodes.summary: Bounded timing and actuator limits are separate requirements of a physical control loop.
nodes.definition: A real-time control loop must meet defined timing deadlines, not merely achieve a high average update rate. Worst-case delays, scheduling jitter, blocking operations, memory allocation, and priority interactions can disrupt execution. Command validation separately checks the actuator interface, units, finite values, position/velocity/effort limits, and freshness. A watchdog can transition to a defined fallback when updates stop. Saturation and rate limits alter closed-loop behavior and must be included in controller analysis. These mechanisms reduce specific failure modes but do not prove whole-robot stability, collision avoidance, or comprehensive safety.
nodes.example: A policy produces joint targets faster than the average required rate but occasionally stalls. A watchdog checks elapsed time independently of that average. Each command is checked against configured joint and rate limits before writing hardware. The actual fallback must suit the robot; blindly setting every target to zero may itself be inappropriate.
nodes.role_en: Connects algorithm outputs and latency measurements to enforceable hardware-interface behavior.

notation.meaning: Requested and admitted interface command.
Configured command limits with interface-specific units.
Optional command-rate limit; actuator capability still requires validation.

nodes.title: 视觉惯性多地图 SLAM
nodes.summary: Feature-based visual, visual-inertial, and multi-map SLAM with place recognition and map merging.
nodes.definition: ORB-SLAM3 is an open-source feature-based SLAM system supporting monocular, stereo, and RGB-D inputs, with visual-inertial configurations and pinhole or fisheye camera models. It combines tracking, local mapping, inertial initialization, place recognition, loop closure, and multi-map management. Maximum a posteriori estimation jointly uses visual and inertial information in its inertial modes. When tracking is lost, the system can create another map and later merge maps when sufficient shared structure is recognized. Its published results apply to specified datasets and sensor configurations, not every robot camera setup.
nodes.example: On a robot head camera, first verify supported image format, intrinsics, camera-IMU transforms, timestamps, and IMU conventions. Evaluate tracking loss, recovery, and trajectory errors under robot motion and field appearance. A successful run on a provided benchmark sequence is evidence about that sequence, not proof that the installed robot is localized reliably.
nodes.role_en: Provides a concrete full-SLAM system extending VIO with revisits, multi-map handling, and global corrections.

notation.meaning: Estimated trajectory, map, and relevant inertial states.
Schematic grouped MAP error terms; exact residuals and configurations are defined in the paper.

paper.contribution: Feature-based visual, visual-inertial and multi-map SLAM with tightly integrated MAP inertial estimation and improved place recognition.

architecture.label: Visual-inertial estimation
architecture.role: Track camera motion with image and optional IMU measurements.

architecture.label: Loop closure and map merging
architecture.role: Recognize revisits and correct or merge maps.

paper.training: The geometric SLAM estimator is not a trained world-model network; the repository supplies the ORB vocabulary used by place recognition.
paper.inference: Track incoming frames, maintain local maps, detect revisits, optimize estimates, and create or merge maps as supported by the configuration.
paper.evaluation: The original paper evaluates multiple sensor modes on EuRoC and TUM-VI. Dataset-specific trajectory results and settings must be read together; no cross-robot guarantee follows.
paper.scale: No neural-network parameter count describes the complete system. Runtime depends on image resolution, features, keyframes, map size, sensor mode, and hardware.
paper.limitations: Needs calibrated and synchronized inputs. Poor visual information, repeated appearance, dynamic scenes, and aggressive motion can cause failure; recovery is not guaranteed.
paper.evidence_level: Original paper metadata and abstract plus official open-source implementation verified.

nodes.title: 直接激光惯性里程计
nodes.summary: Raw-point scan-to-map registration with an iterated Kalman filter and incremental k-d tree.
nodes.definition: FAST-LIO2 is a LiDAR-inertial odometry framework that directly registers raw LiDAR points against a local map rather than requiring a hand-engineered feature-extraction stage. It uses a tightly coupled iterated Kalman-filter formulation and an incremental k-d tree, ikd-Tree, for map search and updates. The design supports different scanning patterns and emphasizes computational efficiency. It remains a geometric state estimator, rather than a learned image-generating world model. The reported operating rates and motion examples are experimental results under stated hardware and data conditions, not universal robot performance specifications.
nodes.example: To integrate FAST-LIO2 with a robot, confirm the supported LiDAR message format, per-point timing, scan pattern, IMU axes, synchronization, and extrinsics. Replay a recorded route and inspect trajectory, map consistency, processing times, and degeneracy. A dense live point-cloud display alone does not establish globally accurate localization or successful loop closure.
nodes.role_en: Exemplifies filter-based LIO and shows why efficient estimation can use geometry and data structures without a large learned dynamics network.

notation.meaning: Raw LiDAR point with appropriate motion compensation.
LiDAR-to-IMU extrinsics.
Local map-plane anchor and normal; representative point-to-plane constraint.

paper.contribution: Direct raw-point registration and incremental ikd-Tree map management within tightly coupled iterated-filter LIO.

architecture.label: LiDAR-inertial odometry
architecture.role: Couple IMU propagation with point-to-map residuals.

architecture.label: Point-cloud timing
architecture.role: Use scan geometry and timing required for motion compensation.

paper.training: The original estimator does not train a neural world model. Configure the sensor model, noise, calibration, and map-processing parameters.
paper.inference: Propagate state with IMU data, register points to the map using iterated updates, and incrementally maintain the searchable map.
paper.evaluation: The paper reports comparisons on 19 public-data sequences and real solid-state LiDAR experiments. It reports up to 100 Hz in particular outdoor experiments; this is not a guaranteed rate on another setup.
paper.scale: Estimator state and local-map data structures determine computation rather than neural-network depth. Check actual implementation, point count, map settings, and processor.
paper.limitations: Local odometry can drift and suffer geometric degeneracy. Timing, extrinsics, point fields, and noise settings matter. The base package should not be presented as guaranteed global loop-closing SLAM.
paper.evidence_level: Original paper and official FAST_LIO repository verified.

nodes.title: 因子图激光惯性平滑建图
nodes.summary: Smoothing combines LiDAR odometry, IMU preintegration, and optional global constraints.
nodes.definition: LIO-SAM formulates LiDAR-inertial odometry and mapping with factor graphs. IMU preintegration supports motion prediction and point-cloud de-skewing; LiDAR registration provides corrections that also constrain inertial bias. The framework can incorporate additional information, including GPS and loop closures, when available and configured. Keyframes and local scan-to-submap matching control computation rather than repeatedly registering against an unrestricted global map. This organization contrasts with filter-based LIO while sharing underlying sensor geometry. Correct driver fields, IMU conventions, calibration, timing, and the chosen repository branch remain essential integration details.
nodes.example: Replay a route containing a genuine revisit. First inspect local LiDAR-inertial trajectory quality, then inspect whether a loop constraint was proposed and geometrically valid. Compare trajectory corrections with independent reference data when possible. A visually closed map after optimization can still be wrong if an accepted loop correspondence was incorrect.
nodes.role_en: Exemplifies smoothing-based LIO and the modular addition of local and global measurement factors.

notation.meaning: Estimated keyframe trajectory and relevant inertial states.
Optional terms only when corresponding valid factors are available; schematic grouping.

paper.contribution: Tightly coupled LiDAR-inertial smoothing and mapping with an extensible factor-graph formulation.

architecture.label: Factor-graph smoothing
architecture.role: Combine relative and available absolute constraints.

architecture.label: LiDAR-inertial processing
architecture.role: Use inertial motion for de-skewing and LiDAR geometry for correction.

architecture.label: Loop constraints
architecture.role: Add revisits when valid and supported by the configured system.

paper.training: No learned neural world model is required by the original method. Sensor calibration, noise models, and pipeline parameters must be configured.
paper.inference: Preintegrate IMU measurements, de-skew scans, estimate keyframe LiDAR odometry, and update smoothing graphs with available constraints.
paper.evaluation: The original paper evaluates data collected from three platforms across different environments and scales. Consult its trajectory references and configurations before comparing with other SLAM systems.
paper.scale: Runtime follows keyframe selection, point processing, local-map size, graph structure, and hardware rather than a neural parameter count.
paper.limitations: Sensor requirements and repository branches differ; confirm support before installation. Geometric degeneracy, poor synchronization, incorrect extrinsics, and false global constraints can degrade results.
paper.evidence_level: Original paper and official implementation verified.

IMU orientation maps vectors between rotating frames.
Angular rates and accelerations are integrated over time.
Noise and bias uncertainty can be modeled probabilistically.
De-skewing composes time-varying rigid transforms.
Each point must have interpretable acquisition timing.
Sensitivity is expressed through derivatives of measurements with respect to parameters.
Singular values reveal weakly constrained parameter directions.

Odometry accumulates relative rigid transforms.
Different motion sensors may contribute complementary measurements.
Image measurements are related to 3D structure through projection.
Inertial propagation requires specific force, angular rate, and bias models.
Camera and IMU measurements must share calibrated spatial relations.
VIO estimates local incremental motion rather than automatically guaranteeing global consistency.
LIO uses scan geometry and motion-corrected point measurements.
The IMU provides propagation and bias-bearing measurements.
Iterated filtering variants extend the nonlinear estimation idea.
LIO estimates an incremental local trajectory.
Factors combine priors and likelihoods into a posterior.
Gaussian residual models yield weighted squared errors.
Nonlinear least-squares solvers linearize residuals using Jacobians.
SLAM provides the trajectory-and-map estimation problem structured by these factors.
A verified revisit becomes a nonlocal factor in the trajectory estimate.
Pose residuals can be expressed in a local tangent space.
Loop constraints correct accumulated local-trajectory inconsistency.
Occupancy evidence is accumulated using a probabilistic sensor model.
Range rays provide occupied and free-space evidence.
Euclidean distance uses a vector norm.
Distance-field gradients guide continuous trajectory optimization.
Depth or range measurements provide surface observations.
A map representation supplies free-space and obstacle evidence.
Global planning searches feasible routes through configuration space.
Local execution must respond to updated state and observations.
Navigation goals commonly use cancellable action interfaces.
Visual networks can extract spatial image features for detection.
Detection and geometric estimation require task-specific held-out metrics.
A detected pixel region must be interpreted through camera projection.
Covariance scales the statistical distance between a prediction and observation.
A Kalman-style prediction provides an innovation and covariance.
Detected objects supply candidate observations requiring identity assignment.
Prediction and update combine uncertain dynamics with observations.
Only suitably associated observations should update an existing object track.
Object measurements and robot motion must be expressed in compatible frames.
Delay calculations require valid timestamps and comparable clocks.
Forward prediction uses a state estimate and motion model.
Delayed observations change the state used to generate a feedback command.
Limits and timing must be applied at the actual hardware command interface.
Control deadlines must account for observation and computation delays.
Saturation and delayed updates can alter controller behavior.
Inertial configurations jointly use camera and IMU constraints.
MAP and bundle-adjustment objectives combine sparse measurement constraints.
Revisit recognition supports loop closure and map merging.
FAST-LIO2 couples inertial prediction with point-to-map constraints.
Its iterated filter repeatedly linearizes the measurement update.
Incremental map indexing affects search and update computation.
LiDAR registration and inertial propagation supply complementary constraints.
Smoothing organizes these constraints as factors over shared states.
Verified revisits can provide global trajectory constraints.
